nameStory: The Agassiz Clam Shrimp gets its name from its striking resemblance to a tiny clam, complete with a hinged, bivalve shell that can snap shut. It's named after Louis Agassiz, a famous 19th-century naturalist who studied many freshwater creatures. Despite its name and clam-like appearance, it's actually a crustacean more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to any mollusk.
description: The Agassiz Clam Shrimp is a fascinating little freshwater crustacean that looks like someone shrunk a clam down to the size of a large pea. These translucent creatures have two hinged shell halves (called valves) that protect their segmented, shrimp-like body inside. They typically grow to about half an inch long and swim upside-down through temporary pools with a graceful, fluttering motion. Their bodies are usually clear to pale yellow, making them seem almost ghostly as they glide through the water.

idTips.label: Hinged bivalve shell
idTips.description: Two clear, oval shell halves connected by a flexible hinge that can open and close like a clam - this is the most distinctive feature that separates them from other small pond creatures

idTips.label: Upside-down swimming
idTips.description: Swims belly-up with a characteristic fluttering motion, using numerous leaf-like legs that create rippling waves along its underside

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Shell and body are nearly transparent with a slight yellowish tint, allowing you to see internal organs and food particles moving through their digestive system

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About the size of a small fingernail (quarter to half inch), with an oval shell that feels smooth and slightly flexible when gently touched

idTips.label: Temporary pool habitat
idTips.description: Found in seasonal pools that dry up completely - if the water body is permanent, you're probably looking at something else

habitat: Agassiz Clam Shrimp live in temporary pools and seasonal wetlands that fill with spring snowmelt or heavy rains and then dry up completely during summer or fall. Look for them in shallow woodland pools, flooded farm fields, roadside ditches, and marshy depressions in meadows throughout New England. They prefer areas with fine sediment and decaying plant matter where they can filter-feed on algae and organic particles.

seasonality.spring: Most active period when they hatch from drought-resistant eggs and can be seen swimming in newly filled temporary pools. Adults are easiest to spot during warm spring days.
seasonality.summer: May still be present in pools that haven't dried up yet, but many populations complete their lifecycle and disappear as pools evaporate. Late summer finds mostly empty shells.
seasonality.fall: Generally absent as adults, though some late-season pools may support a second generation. Eggs remain dormant in dried mud waiting for next year's floods.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent as active animals. Eggs survive frozen in dried sediment, incredibly resistant to both freezing temperatures and drought conditions.

funFact: Agassiz Clam Shrimp are "living time capsules" - their eggs can survive being completely dried out and frozen for decades, then instantly spring to life when the pool fills again, meaning you might be watching creatures hatch from eggs that were laid before you were born!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small freshwater clams or mussels, but clam shrimp actively swim around while true clams stay put on the bottom. Remember: if it's zipping around upside-down, it's a clam shrimp; if it's just sitting there filtering water, it's probably a real clam.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "clam shrimp," these creatures are neither clams nor true shrimp - they're actually ancient crustaceans called branchiopods that have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years. The shell-like covering is technically called a carapace, not a true shell like mollusks have.
compareHints: Since Agassiz Clam Shrimp is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other clam shrimp in the family Limnadiidae by looking for the distinctly oval shell shape and relatively large size. Other regional clam shrimp tend to be smaller and rounder, while Agassiz Clam Shrimp has a more elongated, kidney-shaped outline when viewed from above.
